cse-2021-1-cs-35.approach: Test each statement against a known inequality or a tiny counterexample: $S_1$ contradicts Cauchy–Schwarz, and $S_2$ fails because its right side can never be negative.

steps.title: S1 against Cauchy–Schwarz
steps.body:
The left side is $(\operatorname{Cov}[X,Y])^2$. By Cauchy–Schwarz, $\left(\mathbb{E}[UV]\right)^2 \le \mathbb{E}[U^2]\,\mathbb{E}[V^2]$ with $U = X-\mathbb{E}X$, $V = Y-\mathbb{E}Y$, so
$$(\operatorname{Cov}[X,Y])^2 \le \operatorname{Var}[X]\operatorname{Var}[Y].$$
Strict $>$ is impossible for every pair, so $S_1$ is **false**.

steps.title: S2 by counterexample
steps.body: The right side $\mathbb{E}\big[|X-\mathbb{E}X|\,|Y-\mathbb{E}Y|\big] \ge 0$ always. Take $Y = -X$ with $X = \pm1$ equally likely: $\operatorname{Cov}[X,Y] = -\operatorname{Var}[X] = -1$, while the right side is $\mathbb{E}[1\cdot 1] = 1$. $-1 \ne 1$, so $S_2$ is **false**.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: Both statements are false → option (D).

answer.value: Both S1 and S2 are false

optionAnalysis.reason: $S_1$ violates Cauchy–Schwarz and $S_2$ fails for negatively correlated variables.
$S_1$ is false: $\operatorname{Cov}^2 \le \operatorname{Var}[X]\operatorname{Var}[Y]$ for all $X, Y$.
$S_2$ is false: covariance can be negative, the right side cannot.
Both statements fail, as shown.

pitfalls: Reading $S_1$ as "≥" (equality is possible when $Y$ is a linear function of $X$, but strict > never is).
Forgetting that covariance can be negative while an expectation of absolute values cannot.
cse-2021-1-cs-35.verification: With $Y=-X$, $X=\pm1$: $\operatorname{Cov}^2 = 1 = \operatorname{Var}X\operatorname{Var}Y$, so even the extreme case only reaches equality.

cse-2021-1-cs-36.approach: $N$ joins two vertices exactly when their distance in $G$ is 1 or 2, so $G_2$ is the square of $G$. A shortest path of length $d$ in $G$ can be walked two edges at a time, giving $\lceil d/2 \rceil$.

steps.title: What N encodes
steps.body: $(M^2)_{ij}$ counts walks of length 2 from $i$ to $j$. So $N_{ij} = 1$ iff $\operatorname{dist}_G(i,j) \in \{1, 2\}$ (or a 2-walk $i\to k\to i$, which only affects the diagonal). $G_2 = G^2$.

steps.title: Distances in G²
steps.body: If $\operatorname{dist}_G(u,v) = d$, take a shortest path $u = x_0, x_1, \dots, x_d = v$. The vertices $x_0, x_2, x_4, \dots$ are adjacent in $G_2$, so $\operatorname{dist}_{G_2}(u,v) \le \lceil d/2 \rceil$. Each $G_2$ edge covers at most 2 edges of $G$, so also $\ge \lceil d/2 \rceil$. Hence $\operatorname{dist}_{G_2} = \lceil d/2 \rceil$.

steps.title: Diameter
steps.body: Maximising over all pairs: $\operatorname{diam}(G_2) = \lceil \operatorname{diam}(G)/2 \rceil$, which satisfies option (A)'s "$\le$".

optionAnalysis.reason: Equality $\operatorname{diam}(G_2) = \lceil \operatorname{diam}(G)/2\rceil$ holds, so "$\le$" is true.
$\operatorname{diam}(G_2)$ equals $\lceil \operatorname{diam}(G)/2\rceil$, never strictly greater.
Fails for a path on 3 vertices: $\operatorname{diam}(G)=2$, $\operatorname{diam}(G_2)=1$.
Adding edges can never increase distances.

pitfalls: Thinking $M^2$ alone defines $G_2$ — the "or $M_{ij} > 0$" keeps the original edges too.
cse-2021-1-cs-36.verification: Path $P_5$ (diameter 4): in $P_5^2$ the end vertices are 2 apart, $= \lceil 4/2 \rceil$.

steps.title: Negative j
steps.body: For $j = -3, -2, -1$ the left operand \`j >= 0\` is false, so \`i++\` is **not** evaluated. $i = 0$, count $= 0$.

steps.title: j = 0
steps.body: \`j >= 0\` is true, so \`i++\` runs: it yields $0$ (false) and makes $i = 1$. Body skipped; count $= 0$.

steps.title: j = 1, 2, 3
steps.body: \`i++\` yields $1, 2, 3$ (all true), leaving $i = 2, 3, 4$. count $= 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 6$.

steps.title: After the loop

count = 1 + 2 + 3 = 6, then + i (= 4) gives 10.

cse-2021-1-cs-38.approach: Build the standard 4-state DFA for "ends with 011" (state = longest suffix that is a prefix of 011) and compare the transitions out of the accepting state, where the options differ.

steps.title: States
steps.body: Let $s_0 = \varepsilon$, $s_1 = $ "0", $s_2 = $ "01", $s_3 = $ "011" (accepting) track the longest suffix of the input that is a prefix of 011. All options share: $s_0 \xrightarrow{1} s_0$, $s_0 \xrightarrow{0} s_1$, $s_1 \xrightarrow{0} s_1$, $s_1 \xrightarrow{1} s_2$, $s_2 \xrightarrow{0} s_1$, $s_2 \xrightarrow{1} s_3$.

steps.title: Out of the accepting state
steps.body: After …011: reading **0** gives …0110, whose longest useful suffix is "0" → $s_1$. Reading **1** gives …0111, which ends in no prefix of 011 except $\varepsilon$ → $s_0$.

optionAnalysis.reason: The 1-loop on the accepting state accepts 0111, which does not end in 011.
The accepting state is a trap, so it accepts every string containing 011, e.g. 0110.
On 1 the accepting state goes to the "01" state, so 0111 then 1 reaches acceptance: 01111 is accepted wrongly.
Every transition matches the suffix-tracking DFA.

pitfalls: Confusing "ends with 011" with "contains 011" (option B).
cse-2021-1-cs-38.verification: Run D on 0111 (s1, s2, s3, s0: rejected) and on 1011 (s0, s1, s2, s3: accepted).

cse-2021-1-cs-39.approach: Within 2021 steps a TM can read at most the first 2021 input symbols, so its behaviour for 2021 steps depends only on inputs of length ≤ 2021 — a finite set we can simulate.

steps.title: Key observation
steps.body: In its first 2021 steps the head visits at most 2021 cells. So whether $M$ runs more than 2021 steps on $w$ depends only on the first 2021 symbols of $w$: any $w$ with $|w| > 2021$ behaves like its prefix of length 2021 padded as seen by the head (the head never reaches the rest).

steps.title: Decide L₁ and L₂
steps.body:
Enumerate all inputs of length $\le 2022$ (finitely many, $\sum_{k\le 2022} |\Sigma|^k$) and simulate $M$ on each for 2022 steps.
- $L_1$: accept iff $M$ is still running after step 2021 on **every** such input.
- $L_2$: accept iff it is still running on **some** such input.

Both procedures always halt, so both languages are decidable.

optionAnalysis.reason: Bounded-step questions reduce to finitely many bounded simulations.
$L_2$ is decidable by the same bounded search.
$L_1$ is decidable: checking finitely many representative inputs suffices.
Rice's theorem does not apply — "takes more than 2021 steps" is a property of the machine, not of the language it accepts.

pitfalls: Applying Rice's theorem to a property about running time, not the recognised language.
cse-2021-1-cs-39.verification: Same argument as the classic "M halts within k steps on some input" being decidable.

cse-2021-1-cs-41.approach: Use the standard DFS-tree characterisation of articulation points and look for small counterexamples for the other claims.

steps.title: The root (A, B)
steps.body: An undirected DFS has no cross edges, so different subtrees of the root are joined only through the root. Root is a cut vertex **iff** it has ≥ 2 children. A path $a-b-c$ explored from $b$ gives a root with 2 children that is a cut vertex, so (A) is false and (B) is true.

steps.title: Leaves (C)
steps.body: Deleting a leaf of $T$ leaves the rest of $T$ intact and spanning the other vertices, so the graph stays connected. A leaf is never an articulation point: (C) false.

steps.title: Ancestor/descendant paths (D)
steps.body: Let $u$ have two child subtrees: subtree 1 has a back edge to $u$'s parent $x$, subtree 2 does not (so $u$ is a cut vertex). For $y$ in subtree 1, the path $x \to y$ via the back edge avoids $u$. (D) is false.

optionAnalysis.reason: In a path a–b–c rooted at b, the root is an articulation point.
Standard result: no cross edges in undirected DFS, so subtrees connect only via the root.
Removing a leaf keeps the remaining DFS tree connected.
A descendant in a subtree with a back edge above $u$ is reachable from the ancestor without $u$.

pitfalls: Reading (D) as the definition of a cut vertex — it only holds for descendants in the "separated" child subtree.
cse-2021-1-cs-41.verification: Example for D: edges x–u, u–y, y–x, u–z. DFS x, u, y, then z. u is a cut vertex (z isolated), but x–y is a direct edge.

steps.title: Where F = 1

cse-2021-1-cs-43.approach: Derive symmetry and transitivity from circularity plus the given property, and use the empty relation as the counterexample for non-reflexive cases.

steps.title: Reflexive + circular (C)
steps.body: Symmetric: from $aRb$ and $bRb$ (reflexive), circularity gives $bRa$. Transitive: from $aRb$, $bRc$ circularity gives $cRa$, and symmetry gives $aRc$. So S is an equivalence relation: (C) true.

steps.title: The other options
steps.body:
- (A) reflexive + symmetric need not be transitive: $\{(1,1),(2,2),(3,3),(1,2),(2,1),(2,3),(3,2)\}$ lacks $(1,3)$.
- (B), (D): the empty relation on $\{1\}$ is symmetric, transitive and (vacuously) circular, but not reflexive.

optionAnalysis.reason: Transitivity is missing (counterexample above).
Circular + symmetric gives transitivity but not reflexivity (empty relation).
Reflexivity + circularity yield symmetry and transitivity.
The empty relation is transitive and circular but not reflexive.

pitfalls: Forgetting vacuous truth: the empty relation satisfies every "if … then" property.

cse-2021-1-cs-44.approach: After a reboot the server has no state for the old connection: anything the client sends is answered with RST, nothing is sent spontaneously, and the port is free to be bound again.

steps.title: Client that only waits (A)
steps.body: The rebooted server knows nothing of the connection and sends nothing. Without keepalive, a client that is only reading never sends a segment, so it can wait forever. (A) possible.

steps.title: Server side (B, C, D)
steps.body:
- (B) After reboot the server application can bind and listen on port P again — possible.
- (C) A segment for a connection the host does not know is answered with RST — possible.
- (D) FIN is sent only by an endpoint closing a connection it knows about; the rebooted host has no such connection, so no FIN.

optionAnalysis.reason: No keepalive and no data from the client → no segment ever reveals the dead connection.
The old socket died with the crash; listening on P again is normal.
TCP replies RST to a segment that does not belong to any existing connection.
FIN requires an orderly close of a known connection; the server has lost that state.

pitfalls: Assuming the server "closes" the old connection with FIN after reboot.
cse-2021-1-cs-44.verification: Matches RFC 793 behaviour for half-open connections.

cse-2021-1-cs-45.approach: Fragment payloads must be multiples of 8 bytes and fit MTU − 20; only the first fragment carries the TCP header, and fragments are never retransmitted by routers.
cse-2021-1-cs-45.given:
| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| IP datagram from P | 1400 + 20 = 1420 B |
| MTU R→Q | 820 B |

steps.title: Fragment at R
steps.body: Max data per fragment $= 820 - 20 = 800$ (a multiple of 8). $1400 = 800 + 600$, so two fragments: $800 + 20 = 820$ B and $600 + 20 = 620$ B. (A) true.

steps.title: Loss of a fragment
steps.body: Routers do not buffer or retransmit fragments, so (B) is false. Q cannot reassemble the datagram and discards it; TCP at P times out and retransmits the whole 1400-byte segment (with a new IP datagram). (C) true.

steps.title: Ports
steps.body: The TCP header (with ports) is in the first 20 bytes of the payload, i.e. in fragment 1 only. (D) false.

optionAnalysis.reason: 800 + 600 data bytes; second datagram 600 + 20 = 620 B.
IP routers keep no copies of forwarded fragments.
Only TCP at P recovers losses, by resending the whole segment.
The TCP header is in the first fragment (offset 0).

pitfalls: Forgetting the 20-byte IP header when computing the 1420-byte datagram and its 800-byte split.
cse-2021-1-cs-45.verification: Offsets: fragment 1 offset 0, MF = 1; fragment 2 offset $800/8 = 100$, MF = 0.

cse-2021-1-cs-46.approach: S = 5 lets at most two threads (2 units each) be inside at once, but a thread can be stuck holding one unit; check each claimed outcome with an explicit schedule.

steps.title: Deadlock (D)
steps.body: All five threads execute the first `wait(S)`: S drops 5 → 0. Each now blocks on its second `wait(S)` and nobody can signal. Deadlock of all threads — possible.

steps.title: counter = 5 (A)
steps.body: Run threads one after another: each does two waits, `counter++`, two signals. Final value 5 — possible.

steps.title: counter = 1 (B)
steps.body: Thread T1 enters (S = 3), reads counter = 0 and is pre-empted. T2…T5 each enter one at a time (S = 3 → 1 → 3), incrementing counter to 4. T1 resumes and writes 0 + 1 = 1. Final value 1 — possible.

steps.title: counter = 0 (C)
steps.body: Every `counter++` writes (value read) + 1 ≥ 1, and if all threads complete, at least one write happens last. The final value is ≥ 1, so 0 is impossible.

optionAnalysis.reason: Serial execution gives 5.
One thread's stale read of 0 overwriting the other four increments gives 1.
The last write is always some read value + 1 ≥ 1.
All five first waits succeed, all second waits block.

pitfalls: Assuming S = 5 serialises the increment — it allows two threads at once, so updates can be lost.
cse-2021-1-cs-46.verification: In the schedule for (B), at most two threads are in the critical region at any time (T1 + one other), consistent with S = 5.

cse-2021-1-cs-49.approach: Utilisation of a sliding window $= \dfrac{W\,T_t}{T_t + 2T_p + T_{ack}}$; set it to 0.5 and solve for $W$.

|---|---|
| Data frame $T_t$ | 2000 / 10⁶ = 2 ms |
| ACK $T_{ack}$ | 10 / 10⁶ = 0.01 ms |
| $T_p$ | 100 ms |

steps.title: Cycle time
steps.body: Time from the start of a frame until its ACK is fully received: $T_t + 2T_p + T_{ack} = 2 + 200 + 0.01 = 202.01$ ms.

steps.body: $q_0 \to q_1$ pushes #. In $q_1$ each $a$ pushes A ($n$ times). In $q_2$ each $b$ pops an A ($m \le n$). The move to accepting $q_3$ needs A on top, i.e. $m < n$. Input must be fully read, so $L = \{a^n b^m \mid 0 \le m < n\}$.

steps.body: $n + m = 100$ with $m < n \Rightarrow m < 50$, so $m \in \{0, 1, \dots, 49\}$: **50** strings.
